prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Prove that $[A,A]=0$ and $[A,B]=-[B,A]$.

solutions.title: Expand
solutions.body: $[A,A]=AA-AA=0$ and $[A,B]=AB-BA=-(BA-AB)=-[B,A]$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Prove that $[A,BC]=B[A,C]+[A,B]C$ and $[A,bB+cC]=b[A,B]+c[A,C]$ for operators $A,B,C$ and numbers $b,c$.

solutions.title: Expand
solutions.body:
$B[A,C]+[A,B]C=BAC-BCA+ABC-BAC=ABC-BCA=A(BC)-(BC)A=[A,BC]$.

$[A,bB+cC]=A(bB+cC)-(bB+cC)A=bAB+cAC-bBA-cCA=b[A,B]+c[A,C]$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Prove the Jacobi identity: $[A,[B,C]]+[B,[C,A]]+[C,[A,B]]=0$.
answer: Expand all six products and cancel.

solutions.title: Expand
solutions.body: $[A,[B,C]]=ABC-ACB-BCA+CBA$. Cyclically, $[B,[C,A]]=BCA-BAC-CAB+ACB$ and $[C,[A,B]]=CAB-CBA-ABC+BAC$. Adding the three, each of the six words $ABC,ACB,BCA,BAC,CAB,CBA$ occurs once with a $+$ sign and once with a $-$ sign, so the total is $0$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Suppose $[A,B]=0$. If $n$ is a positive integer, prove that $[A^n,B]=0$.

solutions.title: Induction
solutions.body:
We use $[XY,Z]=X[Y,Z]+[X,Z]Y$ (check: $XYZ-ZXY=X(YZ-ZY)+(XZ-ZX)Y$). The case $n=1$ is the hypothesis. If $[A^{n-1},B]=0$, then
$$[A^n,B]=[A\cdot A^{n-1},B]=A[A^{n-1},B]+[A,B]A^{n-1}=0+0=0.\ ∎$$

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Three operators $(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ form an *angular momentum algebra* if $[J_1,J_2]=iJ_3$, $[J_2,J_3]=iJ_1$, $[J_3,J_1]=iJ_2$ (where $i=\sqrt{-1}$). Put $J_\pm=J_1\pm iJ_2$ and $J^2=J_1^2+J_2^2+J_3^2$. Prove that $[J_3,J_+]=J_+$, $[J_3,J_-]=-J_-$ and $[J_+,J_-]=2J_3$.

*Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Three operators $(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ form an *angular momentum algebra* if $[J_1,J_2]=iJ_3$, $[J_2,J_3]=iJ_1$, $[J_3,J_1]=iJ_2$ (where $i=\sqrt{-1}$). Put $J_\pm=J_1\pm iJ_2$ and $J^2=J_1^2+J_2^2+J_3^2$. Prove that $[J^2,J_i]=0$ for $i=1,2,3$.

solutions.title: Check $i=1$
solutions.body:
By the cyclic symmetry of the relations it suffices to take $i=1$. Using $[XY,Z]=X[Y,Z]+[X,Z]Y$ and $[J_1^2,J_1]=0$:
$$[J_2^2,J_1]=J_2[J_2,J_1]+[J_2,J_1]J_2=-iJ_2J_3-iJ_3J_2,\qquad[J_3^2,J_1]=J_3[J_3,J_1]+[J_3,J_1]J_3=iJ_3J_2+iJ_2J_3.$$
The sum is $0$, so $[J^2,J_1]=0$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Three operators $(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ form an *angular momentum algebra* if $[J_1,J_2]=iJ_3$, $[J_2,J_3]=iJ_1$, $[J_3,J_1]=iJ_2$ (where $i=\sqrt{-1}$). Put $J_\pm=J_1\pm iJ_2$ and $J^2=J_1^2+J_2^2+J_3^2$. Suppose $J^2A=\alpha A$ and $J_3A=\beta A$ where $A$ is an operator and $\alpha,\beta$ are complex numbers. Prove that $J^2(J_\pm A)=\alpha(J_\pm A)$ and $J_3(J_\pm A)=(\beta\pm1)(J_\pm A)$ (all $+$ signs or all $-$ signs).

solutions.title: Move $J_\pm$ to the left
solutions.body:
By Problem 3(b), $[J^2,J_\pm]=0$, so $J^2J_\pm=J_\pm J^2$ and $J^2(J_\pm A)=J_\pm(J^2A)=J_\pm(\alpha A)=\alpha(J_\pm A)$.

By Problem 3(a), $J_3J_\pm=J_\pm J_3\pm J_\pm$. Hence $J_3(J_\pm A)=J_\pm J_3A\pm J_\pm A=\beta J_\pm A\pm J_\pm A=(\beta\pm1)(J_\pm A)$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Three operators $(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ form an *angular momentum algebra* if $[J_1,J_2]=iJ_3$, $[J_2,J_3]=iJ_1$, $[J_3,J_1]=iJ_2$ (where $i=\sqrt{-1}$). Put $J_\pm=J_1\pm iJ_2$ and $J^2=J_1^2+J_2^2+J_3^2$. Suppose $A$ is an operator with $[J_3,A]=kA$ where $k$ is a non-negative integer. Write $T_k=A$ and define $T_{q-1}=[J_-,T_q]$ for $q=k,k-1,k-2,\dots$. Prove that $[J_3,T_q]=qT_q$.
answer: Induction downward on $q$ using the Jacobi identity.

solutions.title: Induction with the Jacobi identity
solutions.body:
For $q=k$ this is the hypothesis. Assume $[J_3,T_q]=qT_q$. The Jacobi identity with $(J_3,J_-,T_q)$ gives
$$[J_3,[J_-,T_q]]=-[J_-,[T_q,J_3]]-[T_q,[J_3,J_-]].$$
Now $[T_q,J_3]=-qT_q$ and $[J_3,J_-]=-J_-$ (Problem 3(a)). So
$$[J_3,T_{q-1}]=-[J_-,-qT_q]-[T_q,-J_-]=q[J_-,T_q]+[T_q,J_-]=q[J_-,T_q]-[J_-,T_q]=(q-1)T_{q-1}.\ ∎$$

prompt: The exponential of an operator is $\exp(A)=I+A+\frac{A^2}{2!}+\frac{A^3}{3!}+\cdots$. Let $X,Y$ be non-commuting operators and $M_n=\left(\exp\frac Xn\exp\frac Yn\right)^n$. Find $a,b,c,d,e,f,g$ if after expanding $M_2$ we get $M_2=aI+bX+cY+dX^2+eXY+fYX+gY^2+\cdots$ (no proof necessary).

solutions.title: Expand $e^{X/2}e^{Y/2}e^{X/2}e^{Y/2}$
solutions.body:
Write $M_2=e^{X/2}e^{Y/2}e^{X/2}e^{Y/2}$ and call the four factors $1,2,3,4$ (factors $1,3$ in $X$; factors $2,4$ in $Y$).

- $I$: coefficient $1$.
- $X$: from factor $1$ or $3$, each $\frac12$: $b=1$. Likewise $c=1$.
- $X^2$: both $X$'s from the same factor: $2\cdot\frac12\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac14$; one from each of factors $1,3$: $\frac14$. So $d=\frac12$. Likewise $g=\frac12$.
- $XY$ (an $X$ before a $Y$): $(X_1,Y_2)$, $(X_1,Y_4)$, $(X_3,Y_4)$, each $\frac14$: $e=\frac34$.
- $YX$ ($Y$ before $X$): only $(Y_2,X_3)$: $f=\frac14$.

**Answer: $(a,b,c,d,e,f,g)=(1,1,1,\tfrac12,\tfrac34,\tfrac14,\tfrac12)$**

prompt: The exponential of an operator is $\exp(A)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{A^k}{k!}$. For non-commuting operators $X,Y$ let $M_n=\left(\exp\frac Xn\exp\frac Yn\right)^n$. Suppose $n$ is a positive integer. Find, with proof, the expansions of $M_n$ and of $\exp(X+Y)$ to second order and show that their difference goes to zero as $n\to\infty$.

solutions.title: Count the ways
solutions.body:
$M_n$ is a product of $2n$ factors $e^{X/n},e^{Y/n},\dots$ (alternately), $n$ of each.

- Order $0$: $I$.
- Order $1$: choose one $\frac Xn$ among $n$ factors: $n\cdot\frac1n=1$, so $X$; likewise $Y$.
- $X^2$: take $\frac Xn$ from two different $X$-factors: $\binom n2\frac1{n^2}$; or $\frac{1}{2!}\left(\frac Xn\right)^2$ from one factor: $n\cdot\frac1{2n^2}$. Total $\frac{n(n-1)}{2n^2}+\frac1{2n}=\frac12$. Likewise $Y^2$ has coefficient $\frac12$.
- $XY$ (an $X$ to the left of a $Y$): if the $Y$ comes from the $j$-th $Y$-factor, an $X$ may come from any of the $j$ $X$-factors before it, so the coefficient is $\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{j}{n^2}=\frac{n+1}{2n}=\frac12+\frac1{2n}$.
- $YX$: if the $Y$ comes from the $j$-th $Y$-factor, an $X$ to its right can come from the $n-j$ later $X$-factors: $\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{n-j}{n^2}=\frac{n-1}{2n}=\frac12-\frac1{2n}$.

On the other side, $\exp(X+Y)=I+(X+Y)+\frac12(X+Y)^2+\cdots=I+X+Y+\frac12X^2+\frac12XY+\frac12YX+\frac12Y^2+\cdots$.

The difference of the second-order expansions is $\frac{1}{2n}XY-\frac1{2n}YX=\frac{XY-YX}{2n}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. ∎

prompt: For non-commuting operators $X,Y$, let $M_2=\exp\frac X2\exp\frac Y2\exp\frac X2\exp\frac Y2$, where $\exp(A)=\sum_k\frac{A^k}{k!}$. Find, with proof, the coefficient of $X^{10}Y^{10}$ (the word $XX\cdots XYY\cdots Y$) in the expansion of $M_2$.

For non-commuting operators $X,Y$, let $M_n=\left(\exp\frac Xn\exp\frac Yn\right)^n$. In the expansion of $M_n$ find, with proof, the coefficient of $(XY)^k=XYXY\cdots XY$ where $k$ is a positive integer.

solutions.title: Reduce to $(I+X)(I+Y)$ and use generating functions
solutions.body:
A term $XYXY\cdots XY$ contains no $X^2$ or $Y^2$ inside a single factor, so only the terms $I$ and $\frac Xn$ (resp. $\frac Yn$) of each exponential matter. We may therefore count in the product $\big((I+X)(I+Y)\big)^n$ and multiply the coefficient by $\frac1{n^{2k}}$ at the end.

In the $n$ blocks $(I+X)(I+Y)$ choose the blocks $b_1<b_2<\cdots<b_k$ from which the $Y$'s of $(XY)^k$ are taken. For the $j$-th $Y$ (from block $b_j$), its $X$ must come from a block $\le b_j$ and strictly after the block of the previous $Y$ (or from the same block as $Y_{j}$ since $(I+X)$ precedes $(I+Y)$ in that block): let $i_j=b_j-b_{j-1}\ge1$ with $b_0=0$, so the $X$ may be chosen in exactly $i_j$ ways (from any of the $i_j$ blocks after $b_{j-1}$ up to and including $b_j$). With $i_{k+1}=n-b_k\ge0$, the coefficient of $(XY)^k$ in $\big((I+X)(I+Y)\big)^n$ is
$$\sum_{\substack{i_1+\cdots+i_{k+1}=n\\ i_1,\dots,i_k\ge1,\ i_{k+1}\ge0}}i_1i_2\cdots i_k,$$
the coefficient of $x^n$ in $\left(x+2x^2+3x^3+\cdots\right)^k\left(1+x+x^2+\cdots\right)=\frac{x^k}{(1-x)^{2k}}\cdot\frac1{1-x}=x^k(1-x)^{-(2k+1)}$. That is the coefficient of $x^{n-k}$ in $(1-x)^{-(2k+1)}$, which is $\binom{n-k+2k}{2k}=\binom{n+k}{2k}$.

Hence the coefficient of $(XY)^k$ in $M_n$ is $\dfrac{\binom{n+k}{2k}}{n^{2k}}$. (Check: $n=3$, $k=2$ gives $\frac{5}{81}$, matching a direct expansion; $k=1$ gives $\frac{n+1}{2n}$, as in Problem 7.) ∎

prompt: The exponential of an operator is $\exp(A)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{A^k}{k!}$. Prove that $\exp((s+t)A)=\exp(sA)\exp(tA)$ for numbers $s,t$ and an operator $A$.
answer: Binomial theorem for the commuting terms $sA$ and $tA$.

solutions.title: Multiply the series
solutions.body:
$$\exp(sA)\exp(tA)=\sum_{m\ge0}\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{s^mt^n}{m!\,n!}A^{m+n}.$$
Group the terms by $k=m+n$ (powers of the single operator $A$ commute with each other):
$$\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{A^k}{k!}\sum_{m=0}^k\binom kms^mt^{k-m}=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(s+t)^kA^k}{k!}=\exp((s+t)A).\ ∎$$

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Let $B_0=B$ and $B_{n+1}=[A,B_n]$ for $n\ge0$. Prove that for $N\ge1$, $$[A^N,B_0]=\sum_{j=1}^N\binom NjB_jA^{N-j}.$$

solutions.title: Induction
solutions.body:
For $N=1$: $[A,B_0]=B_1$. Suppose it holds for $N$. Then, using $[XY,Z]=X[Y,Z]+[X,Z]Y$ and $AB_j=B_{j+1}+B_jA$,
$$[A^{N+1},B_0]=A[A^N,B_0]+[A,B_0]A^N=\sum_{j=1}^N\binom Nj\left(B_{j+1}+B_jA\right)A^{N-j}+B_1A^N.$$
$$=\sum_{j=2}^{N+1}\binom N{j-1}B_jA^{N+1-j}+\sum_{j=1}^N\binom NjB_jA^{N+1-j}+B_1A^N.$$
Collecting the coefficient of $B_jA^{N+1-j}$ for $2\le j\le N$ gives $\binom N{j-1}+\binom Nj=\binom{N+1}j$; for $j=1$ we get $\binom N1+1=\binom{N+1}1$; and for $j=N+1$ we get $\binom NN=\binom{N+1}{N+1}$. So $[A^{N+1},B_0]=\sum_{j=1}^{N+1}\binom{N+1}jB_jA^{N+1-j}$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Let $B_0=B$ and $B_{n+1}=[A,B_n]$ for $n\ge0$. Prove (ignoring issues of convergence) that $$[\exp(A),B_0]=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{B_j}{j!}\exp(A).$$

solutions.title: Use part (a)
solutions.body:
$$[\exp(A),B_0]=\sum_{N\ge0}\frac1{N!}[A^N,B_0]=\sum_{N\ge1}\frac1{N!}\sum_{j=1}^N\binom NjB_jA^{N-j}=\sum_{j\ge1}\sum_{N\ge j}\frac{B_jA^{N-j}}{j!\,(N-j)!}.$$
Setting $M=N-j$, the inner sum is $\frac{B_j}{j!}\sum_{M\ge0}\frac{A^M}{M!}=\frac{B_j}{j!}\exp(A)$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Let $B_0=B$ and $B_{n+1}=[A,B_n]$ for $n\ge0$. Prove (ignoring issues of convergence) that $$\exp(A)\,B\,\exp(-A)=\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{B_j}{j!}.$$
answer: Multiply part (b) on the right by $\exp(-A)$.

solutions.title: Use part (b) and Problem 10
solutions.body:
By Problem 10 with $s=1$, $t=-1$: $\exp(A)\exp(-A)=\exp(0)=I$. Part (b) says $\exp(A)B-B\exp(A)=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{B_j}{j!}\exp(A)$. Multiplying on the right by $\exp(-A)$:
$$\exp(A)B\exp(-A)-B=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{B_j}{j!},$$
and moving $B=B_0$ to the right-hand side gives $\exp(A)B\exp(-A)=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{B_j}{j!}$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Operators $\vec J=(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ *generate vector rotations* on $\vec X=(X_1,X_2,X_3)$ if (1) $\vec J$ forms an angular momentum algebra ($[J_1,J_2]=iJ_3$ and cyclic), (2) $[J_i,X_j]=i\sum_{k=1}^3\epsilon_{ijk}X_k$ for $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$ (where $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol: $\epsilon_{123}=\epsilon_{231}=\epsilon_{312}=1$, $\epsilon_{321}=\epsilon_{213}=\epsilon_{132}=-1$, and $0$ if two indices are equal), and (3) $X_1,X_2,X_3$ are linearly independent. Suppose $\vec J$ generates rotations on $\vec X$. Use the Hadamard lemma $\exp(A)B\exp(-A)=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{B_j}{j!}$ (with $B_0=B$, $B_{n+1}=[A,B_n]$) to prove that $$\exp(-i\theta J_3)\,[x_1X_1+x_2X_2+x_3X_3]\,\exp(i\theta J_3)=a_1X_1+a_2X_2+a_3X_3,$$ where $(a_1,a_2,a_3)=(x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta,\ x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta,\ x_3)$.
answer: Compute the iterated commutators with $A=-i\theta J_3$ and sum the series.

solutions.title: Iterated commutators
solutions.body:
Take $A=-i\theta J_3$ and $B_0=x_1X_1+x_2X_2+x_3X_3$. From $[J_3,X_1]=iX_2$, $[J_3,X_2]=-iX_1$, $[J_3,X_3]=0$:
$$B_1=[A,B_0]=-i\theta\left(x_1\,iX_2+x_2(-i)X_1\right)=\theta(x_1X_2-x_2X_1).$$
$$B_2=[A,B_1]=-i\theta\cdot\theta\left(x_1(-i)X_1-x_2\,iX_2\right)=-\theta^2(x_1X_1+x_2X_2).$$
In general $B_{n+2}=-\theta^2B_n$ for $n\ge1$ (the $X_3$ term of $B_0$ is killed by the first commutator).

Even terms: $B_0+\sum_{k\ge2,\,\text{even}}\frac{B_k}{k!}=x_3X_3+(x_1X_1+x_2X_2)\left(1-\frac{\theta^2}{2!}+\frac{\theta^4}{4!}-\cdots\right)=x_3X_3+(x_1X_1+x_2X_2)\cos\theta.$

Odd terms: $B_1=\theta(x_1X_2-x_2X_1)$, $B_3=-\theta^2B_1,\dots$, so $\sum_{k\text{ odd}}\frac{B_k}{k!}=(x_1X_2-x_2X_1)\left(\theta-\frac{\theta^3}{3!}+\frac{\theta^5}{5!}-\cdots\right)=(x_1X_2-x_2X_1)\sin\theta$.

Adding: $(x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta)X_1+(x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta)X_2+x_3X_3$. ∎

prompt: *Operators* are objects that can be added, multiplied (in general $AB\ne BA$) and multiplied by complex numbers; they obey the usual associative and distributive laws, there is a zero operator $0$ and an identity operator $I$ with $IA=AI=A$. The *commutator* is $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Operators $\vec J=(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ *generate vector rotations* on $\vec X=(X_1,X_2,X_3)$ if (1) $\vec J$ forms an angular momentum algebra ($[J_1,J_2]=iJ_3$ and cyclic), (2) $[J_i,X_j]=i\sum_{k=1}^3\epsilon_{ijk}X_k$ for $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$ (where $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol: $\epsilon_{123}=\epsilon_{231}=\epsilon_{312}=1$, $\epsilon_{321}=\epsilon_{213}=\epsilon_{132}=-1$, and $0$ if two indices are equal), and (3) $X_1,X_2,X_3$ are linearly independent. For a unit vector $\hat n$ and a vector $\vec a$, rotate $\vec a$ about $\hat n$ by an angle $\theta$ to get $\vec b$, defined by $\exp(-i\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec J)\,(\vec a\cdot\vec X)\,\exp(i\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec J)=\vec b\cdot\vec X$, where $\vec v\cdot\vec X=v_1X_1+v_2X_2+v_3X_3$. Prove that $$(\vec b-\vec a)\cdot\vec X=\theta(\hat n\times\vec a)\cdot\vec X+\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{\theta^k\,\vec a_k}{k!}\cdot\vec X,$$ where $\vec a_0=\vec a$ and $\vec a_k=\hat n\times\vec a_{k-1}$.
answer: Apply the Hadamard lemma; the commutator with $-i\theta\hat n\cdot\vec J$ acts as the cross product with $\theta\hat n$.

solutions.title: Hadamard lemma and one commutator
solutions.body:
With $A=-i\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec J$ and $B_0=\vec a\cdot\vec X$, the Hadamard lemma gives $\vec b\cdot\vec X=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{B_j}{j!}$. We compute one commutator of $A$ with a general $\vec v\cdot\vec X$:
$$[-i\theta\sum_in_iJ_i,\ \sum_jv_jX_j]=-i\theta\sum_{i,j}n_iv_j[J_i,X_j]=\theta\sum_{i,j,k}n_iv_j\epsilon_{ijk}X_k=\theta\,(\hat n\times\vec v)\cdot\vec X,$$
since $(\hat n\times\vec v)_k=\sum_{i,j}\epsilon_{ijk}n_iv_j$.

So taking the commutator with $A$ replaces $\vec v$ by $\theta\,\hat n\times\vec v$, and $B_j=\theta^j\,\vec a_j\cdot\vec X$. Therefore $\vec b\cdot\vec X=\vec a\cdot\vec X+\theta(\hat n\times\vec a)\cdot\vec X+\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{\theta^k\vec a_k}{k!}\cdot\vec X$, and subtracting $\vec a\cdot\vec X$ gives the claim (the $X_i$ being linearly independent, this is an identity of coefficient vectors). ∎

prompt: With $\hat n$ a unit vector, $\vec a_0=\vec a$ and $\vec a_k=\hat n\times\vec a_{k-1}$, prove that $$\left|\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{\theta^k\vec a_k}{k!}\right|\le|\vec a|\,\theta^2e^{|\theta|},$$ where $|\vec v|=\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2}$.
answer: $|\vec a_k|\le|\vec a|$, then the triangle inequality and $\frac1{(k+2)!}\le\frac1{k!}$.

solutions.title: Triangle inequality
solutions.body:
Since $\hat n$ is a unit vector, $|\vec a_k|=|\hat n\times\vec a_{k-1}|\le|\hat n||\vec a_{k-1}|=|\vec a_{k-1}|$, so by induction $|\vec a_k|\le|\vec a|$ for all $k$. By the triangle inequality,
$$\left|\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{\theta^k\vec a_k}{k!}\right|\le|\vec a|\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{|\theta|^k}{k!}=|\vec a|\,\theta^2\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{|\theta|^k}{(k+2)!}\le|\vec a|\,\theta^2\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{|\theta|^k}{k!}=|\vec a|\,\theta^2e^{|\theta|}.\ ∎$$

prompt: Let $\vec b$ be the vector obtained by rotating $\vec a$ about the unit axis $\hat n$ by an angle $\theta$. Give a geometric proof of why $\vec b-\vec a\approx\theta\,(\hat n\times\vec a)$ when $\theta$ is much less than one. Clearly identify what approximation(s) you use.
answer: Arc length approximation: $|AB|\approx\theta\cdot AP$ and $AB\perp$ the axis plane, i.e. parallel to $\hat n\times\vec a$.

solutions.title: Arc approximation
solutions.body:
Let $O$ be the origin, $A$ and $B$ the tips of $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, and $P$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the axis through $O$ in direction $\hat n$. Rotation about the axis keeps $P$ fixed and moves $A$ along a circle centred at $P$ in the plane perpendicular to $\hat n$, so $PA=PB$ and $\angle APB=\theta$.

*Approximation 1:* for small $\theta$ the chord $AB$ is approximately the circular arc, so $|\vec b-\vec a|=AB\approx\theta\cdot PA$. Now $PA=OA\sin\angle AOP=|\vec a||\sin\angle(\vec a,\hat n)|=|\hat n\times\vec a|$. So the magnitudes agree: $|\vec b-\vec a|\approx\theta|\hat n\times\vec a|$.

*Approximation 2:* for small $\theta$ the chord $AB$ is almost tangent to the circle at $A$, i.e. $\angle BAP\approx90^\circ$. The tangent at $A$ is perpendicular to both $\hat n$ and to $PA$ (hence to $\vec a$'s component perpendicular to the axis), so it is parallel to $\hat n\times\vec a$, and the sense of the rotation (counterclockwise about $\hat n$) agrees with the direction of $\hat n\times\vec a$.

Together, $\vec b-\vec a\approx\theta\,(\hat n\times\vec a)$. ∎
